interactions.label: A 60-year-old man on warfarin presents with profuse bright-red blood per rectum

params.question: A 60-year-old man on warfarin presents with profuse bright-red blood per rectum and a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. His BUN:creatinine ratio is 28:1. Which is the most likely source of bleeding?

answers.text: Haemorrhoids

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haemorrhoids cause modest, bright-red bleeding and rarely produce haemodynamic instability of this severity.

answers.text: Diverticular disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diverticular bleeding can cause haematochezia and instability, but the BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1 points to an upper source — digested blood raises urea disproportionately.

answers.text: Upper gastrointestinal tract

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Despite haematochezia, the haemodynamic instability and BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1 point to an upper GI source. Massive upper bleeding can produce haematochezia because blood transits too quickly for digestion to melaena.

answers.text: Colorectal malignancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Colorectal cancer typically presents with occult blood loss and chronic anaemia, not acute haemodynamic collapse.

overallFeedback.feedback: The BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1 is the key clue — digested blood raises urea disproportionately, pointing to an upper GI source even when haematochezia is present.
Correct! A BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1 favours an upper source. In any unstable patient with haematochezia, always exclude an upper GI source first.

interactions.label: A cirrhotic patient on propranolol presents with haematemesis. Heart rate is 82

params.question: A cirrhotic patient on propranolol presents with haematemesis. Heart rate is 82 bpm, blood pressure is 92/60 mmHg, serum lactate is 5.2 mmol/L, and haemoglobin is 12.4 g/dL. Which parameter most reliably indicates the severity of blood loss at this stage?

answers.text: Heart rate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-blockers like propranolol suppress the tachycardic response to hypovolaemia, making heart rate unreliable in this patient.

answers.text: Haemoglobin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Compensatory vasoconstriction keeps haematocrit and haemoglobin normal for the first 4–6 hours after haemorrhage. This normal haemoglobin is falsely reassuring.

answers.text: Blood pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blood pressure can be maintained by compensatory vasoconstriction in early shock. A systolic of 92 may already represent decompensation, but blood pressure alone is a late and unreliable marker.

answers.text: Serum lactate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lactate above 4 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion from anaerobic metabolism. Unlike haemoglobin (delayed by haemodilution lag) and heart rate (masked by propranolol), lactate reflects real-time tissue perfusion.

overallFeedback.feedback: Serum lactate is the most reliable parameter here. Haemoglobin is falsely normal for 4–6 hours after haemorrhage, heart rate is masked by propranolol, and blood pressure is a late marker sustained by vasoconstriction.

Correct! Serum lactate is the most reliable early indicator of shock severity. Haemoglobin lags 4–6 hours, heart rate is suppressed by propranolol, and blood pressure is sustained by vasoconstriction in early shock.

interactions.label: A patient with suspected GI bleeding has a lying blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg.

params.question: A patient with suspected GI bleeding has a lying blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. On standing, blood pressure drops to 96/64 mmHg and pulse rises by 24 beats per minute. What does this orthostatic change indicate?

answers.text: Early compensated shock without clinically significant blood loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A systolic drop of 24 mmHg with a pulse rise of 24 bpm exceeds the diagnostic threshold (≥20 mmHg drop, ≥20 bpm rise) and indicates significant hypovolaemia requiring intervention.

answers.text: At least one litre of volume depletion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A systolic drop of ≥20 mmHg and pulse rise of ≥20 bpm on standing signals at least one litre of volume loss. This is the most informative bedside sign for hypovolaemia, yet it is routinely skipped in busy emergency settings.

answers.text: At least two litres of volume depletion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The threshold for a positive orthostatic test corresponds to approximately one litre of volume loss, not two. Two litres of loss would typically produce resting hypotension and other signs of decompensation.

answers.text: Autonomic dysfunction unrelated to bleeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While autonomic neuropathy can cause orthostatic changes, in a patient with suspected GI bleeding these findings must be interpreted as evidence of volume depletion until proven otherwise.

overallFeedback.feedback: A systolic drop ≥20 mmHg and pulse rise ≥20 bpm on standing signals at least one litre of volume depletion. This orthostatic assessment is the most informative bedside sign in GI bleeding.
Correct! Orthostatic hypotension with a systolic drop ≥20 mmHg and pulse rise ≥20 bpm signals at least one litre of volume loss. Never omit this assessment in suspected GI bleeding.

params.question: At upper endoscopy, Patient A has a duodenal ulcer with a spurting artery (Forrest 1a) and Patient B has an ulcer with a clean base (Forrest 3). How should their management differ?

answers.text: Both require endoscopic haemostasis followed by high-dose intravenous PPI

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Forrest 3 (clean base) carries minimal rebleeding risk and does not need endoscopic intervention. Only high-risk lesions such as Forrest 1a require haemostasis.

answers.text: Patient A should proceed directly to surgery; Patient B needs endoscopic haemostasis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Surgery is the last resort in the escalation ladder. Endoscopic haemostasis is the first-line intervention for Forrest 1a, with CT angiography and embolisation as intermediate steps if endoscopy fails.

answers.text: Both can be managed conservatively since proton pump inhibitors alone control most ulcer bleeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Forrest 1a carries approximately 55% rebleeding risk. PPIs alone cannot control active arterial haemorrhage — endoscopic haemostasis is essential before commencing PPI therapy.

answers.text: Patient A needs immediate haemostasis and high-dose PPI; Patient B can be managed conservatively

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Forrest 1a (spurting artery) carries approximately 55% rebleeding risk and demands immediate endoscopic haemostasis followed by high-dose IV PPI. Forrest 3 (clean base) has minimal risk and is managed conservatively.

overallFeedback.feedback: Forrest 1a (spurting artery, ~55% rebleed risk) requires immediate endoscopic haemostasis and high-dose IV PPI. Forrest 3 (clean base, minimal risk) is managed conservatively. The Forrest classification directly determines intervention.

Correct! The Forrest classification directly drives management: high-risk lesions (1a, ~55% rebleed) need endoscopic haemostasis plus high-dose PPI, while low-risk lesions (clean base) need only conservative care.

interactions.label: After endoscopic haemostasis of a high-risk peptic ulcer, what is the primary go

params.question: After endoscopic haemostasis of a high-risk peptic ulcer, what is the primary goal of high-dose intravenous pantoprazole (80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/hour for 72 hours)?

answers.text: To constrict the bleeding vessel and reduce splanchnic blood flow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vasoconstriction is the mechanism of vasoactive drugs like terlipressin, used in variceal bleeding. Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor — it suppresses acid, not blood flow.

answers.text: To eradicate Helicobacter pylori at the ulcer site

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: H. pylori eradication requires dedicated antibiotic therapy over days to weeks and reduces long-term rebleeding by ~80%. Acute high-dose IV PPI aims to stabilise the clot, not eradicate the organism.

answers.text: To raise gastric pH above 6 and stabilise the fibrin clot

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: High-dose continuous PPI raises gastric pH above 6, preventing acid-mediated degradation of the fibrin clot over the ulcer. This is acid suppression for peptic disease — distinct from vasoactive therapy for varices.

answers.text: To reduce portal venous pressure and prevent variceal rebleeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reducing portal pressure is the role of terlipressin acutely and non-selective beta-blockers for prophylaxis in variceal bleeding. PPIs treat peptic ulcer bleeding — confusing the two is a serious clinical error.

overallFeedback.feedback: The primary goal is raising gastric pH above 6 to stabilise the fibrin clot. Pantoprazole is an acid suppressant for peptic disease — confusing it with vasoactive therapy for variceal bleeding is a dangerous clinical error.
Correct! High-dose IV PPI raises gastric pH above 6 to stabilise the fibrin clot. Remember: PPIs treat peptic ulcer bleeding; variceal bleeding requires vasoactive drugs like terlipressin.
